Chapter 3: Generating and Selecting Original Ideas
Let’s dive into something that’s often misunderstood—where original ideas actually come from. You might’ve heard folks say, “Oh, creativity? That’s a rare gift, only a few lucky people have it.” But here’s the real story: coming up with original ideas is a skill. And like any skill, you can get better at it with practice and a bit of persistence.
If you look at original thinkers, they’re not just waiting around for a lightning bolt of inspiration. In fact, they tend to come up with a whole lot of ideas—knowing full well that most won’t work out. It’s a bit like a photographer snapping hundreds of photos just to get that one perfect shot. The secret? Volume. The more ideas you generate, the better your odds of stumbling on something truly novel and valuable.
So, how do you actually spark those original ideas? Well, there are a few habits that can really help:
First, set aside dedicated time for brainstorming. Let your mind wander—don’t judge or censor yourself during this stage. Just let the ideas flow.
Next, draw inspiration from all sorts of places. Read widely. Explore different industries, cultures, and disciplines. Sometimes the best ideas come from the most unexpected sources.
And, don’t forget about collaboration. Working with people who have different perspectives and experiences can lead to sparks you’d never find on your own.
Now, once you’ve got a pool of ideas, the real challenge kicks in—how do you choose which ones to pursue? Honestly, picking the best ideas can be even tougher than generating them. Why? Because we all tend to think our own ideas are brilliant, and it’s easy to miss the value in someone else’s feedback.
To get better at selecting ideas, original thinkers usually do a few things:
They seek out honest feedback from trusted colleagues or mentors—folks who’ll tell them what they really think, not just what they want to hear.
They test ideas in low-risk environments. Instead of going all in, they gather real-world data through small experiments.
And, they stay open to making changes—or even letting go of ideas that aren’t working out the way they hoped.
Here’s a helpful way to picture this process: imagine you’re using a sieve. You pour your ideas in, and little by little, you filter out the ones that aren’t quite right. It’s not about finding “the one” immediately—it’s about refining, improving, and iterating until something really stands out.
Now, let’s talk about organizations. The best ones create spaces where people actually want to experiment—and where failure isn’t a dirty word, but a chance to learn. That might mean regular idea-sharing sessions where everyone’s voice matters, offering resources for quick pilots or prototypes, and celebrating not just wins, but the effort and lessons learned along the way.
There’s one more thing to keep in mind. Originality often comes from connecting old ideas in new ways. Think about it—some of the biggest breakthroughs happened when someone combined familiar concepts from different fields. Take the printing press, for example. It was born by merging movable type with the mechanics of a wine press. Sometimes, real innovation is just about making those unexpected connections.
So, here’s the key takeaway: generating and choosing original ideas is all about exploring, experimenting, and refining as you go. If you embrace the idea of quantity, seek out diverse viewpoints, and aren’t afraid to make changes based on feedback, you’ll put yourself in the best position to make a real impact.
